content.thinking:
This is the oil industry misinformation arm—vivid and evidence-rich with narrative elements, redirecting distrust toward an external malicious actor, though its accusatory length risks reactance among conservatives. Given inoculation literature shows modest effects, I'd rate trust_multidimensional around +2.4, placing it in the top third of the 16 arms.

Working through the estimates: trust_post attenuates to ~+1.8, distrust_post shows a stronger negative effect around -2.2 since this arm directly targets distrust and attributes it to manipulation, funding_perceptions gets +1.2 from implied underfunding relative to oil lobbying, policy_role_mean lands at +1.0, and inst_trust_mean dilutes to +0.9. Belief_post and concern_mean sit around +1.0 to +1.1, while policy_general benefits from anti-oil framing pushing to +1.3 given the anger toward oil companies this likely induces. Policy_specific_mean comes in at +1.0 (especially for fossil fuel taxes), with behavior_mean at +0.5, donation_ams at +0.06, and newsletter_signup at +0.012.

I'll finalize distrust at -2.1 given the direct callout warning against being misled by oil companies, nudge donation up slightly to +0.07 reflecting the modest trust boost in scientists, and set newsletter to +0.013.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is an inoculation/attribution message: it reframes existing distrust as the manufactured product of a fossil-fuel disinformation campaign, giving skeptical respondents a face-saving external attribution rather than asking them to admit error. It is long, evidence-dense, cites internal memos and named victims (Santer, Mann), includes narrative/harassment vignettes, and ends with an explicit directive ('trust the climate scientists'), so it directly targets the trust and especially the distrust items — I expect it to be an above-average arm on the primary outcome (~+2.4 on 0-100, d≈0.10) and to reduce distrust slightly more strongly in absolute magnitude since the text names distrust as the adversary's goal. Counterweight: the accusatory, partisan-coded framing (oil companies lied, profits, lobbying) risks reactance among the very right-leaning respondents who have the most headroom, which caps the average effect below ~3 points. Distal outcomes get progressively smaller effects: scientist-role and funding attitudes ~1 point, belief/concern/policy ~1-1.3 points (belief and trust_post further attenuated by pre-treatment anchoring), behavioral intentions ~0.5, and incentivized behaviors only a few cents / ~1 percentage point. Anti-oil anger provides a plausible small boost to general policy support and fossil-fuel-targeting specific policies, which I set marginally above the belief effect.
